title: 'I Won't Eat From Your Hands': Kerala Chef's Reply to Skin-Tone Troll Goes Viral
excerpt: Chef Karthikeyan answered a troll who mocked his skin tone by listing the prominent guests he has served — a calm rebuttal that turned colourist abuse into a conversation about dignity.
body:
• Chef Karthikeyan, a Kerala-based chef, was targeted by an online troll who mocked his skin tone, writing "Aapka haath bahut kala hai" (your hand is very dark) and declaring "main nahi khaunga apke hath ka" — I won't eat food cooked by your hands.
  • Instead of ignoring the comment, the chef hit back, responding by listing the prominent guests he has served over his career.
  • His reply went viral, with Mathrubhumi, The Indian Express, Hindustan Times, Asianet Newsable and India Today all picking up the story.
  • The episode has been widely held up as an example of why confronting colourism and racist bullying can be more powerful than staying silent.

A Kerala chef's calm, cutting response to a troll who mocked his skin tone has gone viral — and turned an ugly comment into a wider conversation about colourism. Chef Karthikeyan was targeted online after a troll remarked on the colour of his hands and declared he would not eat food prepared by him. Rather than let it pass, the chef answered back, listing the prominent guests he has served through his career.

The exchange, first reported by Mathrubhumi English and quickly picked up by The Indian Express, Hindustan Times, Asianet Newsable and India Today, struck a nerve far beyond food circles. "'I won't eat from your hands': Chef hits back at skin-colour troll," ran The Indian Express headline. Hindustan Times put it more directly: the chef "shuts down" the troll who told him "main nahi khaunga apke hath ka" and remarked on his skin colour.

What the troll said

The comment was as crude as it was revealing. "Aapka haath bahut kala hai" — your hand is very dark — the troll wrote, pairing the remark about the chef's skin tone with the declaration that he would not eat anything cooked by those hands. It was, in other words, not a critique of the cooking but of the cook's complexion: colourism stated plainly, in the comments section of a working chef's page.

Colourism of this kind is depressingly familiar in India, where fairness-cream advertising and matrimonial ads have long equated lighter skin with beauty, status and employability. What made this episode different was the reply.

The response

Chef Karthikeyan did not argue, apologise or delete. He answered the insult with his record: a list of the prominent guests he has served, letting his professional standing do the talking. The troll's premise — that dark skin disqualifies a pair of hands from a kitchen — collapsed against a career of feeding people who matter.

"Main nahi khaunga apke hath ka" — I won't eat food cooked by your hands.

— the troll's comment, as reported by Hindustan Times

The reply travelled fast. Mathrubhumi English's report, headlined "'This dark-skinned chef…' Kerala chef's reply to troll sparks online buzz," captured the mood of the reaction: amusement at the comeback, and something closer to admiration for the refusal to absorb the insult quietly.

Why it resonated

The Indian Express framed the episode as a lesson in itself, noting that Chef Karthikeyan's response "highlights why speaking up against colourism and racist bullying can be more powerful than simply ignoring online hate."

"Speaking up against colourism and racist bullying can be more powerful than simply ignoring online hate."

— The Indian Express

The point lands because the usual advice given to targets of online abuse — don't feed the trolls, don't dignify it — asks the victim to carry the cost of silence while the insult stands unchallenged. Karthikeyan's approach inverted that logic. He did not escalate; he documented. And in doing so he shifted the story from one man's complexion to the absurdity of judging a chef by anything other than his food.

For Kerala's food world, the episode also carries a particular irony. The state's cuisine — from Malabar biryanis to Syrian Christian appams to the toddy-shop curries now celebrated by food writers — was built by exactly the working hands the troll sneered at. The hands that pound coconut, temper mustard seeds and slow-cook fish moilee were never the point of the prejudice, and never will be the measure of the cooking.

The diaspora angle

Colourism travels. Diaspora Indians encounter it in casting rooms and workplaces abroad, in the skin-lightening products still stocked on South Asian grocery shelves, and in the comments sections of every prominent brown creator. A chef in Kerala answering a colourist troll with his résumé is a small story with a large echo.

What's next

The troll has not been publicly identified, and there is no indication the chef intends to pursue the matter further — the response itself was the verdict. What endures is the template: a working professional, confronted with bigotry dressed up as opinion, answering with facts about his own worth. In a week of viral outrages, this one may actually leave something behind — the quiet suggestion that the best response to "your hands are too dark" is simply to keep cooking, and to say so.
nri_angle: Colourism travels with the diaspora, showing up in casting, workplaces and South Asian grocery aisles abroad; the chef's calm, factual rebuttal resonates across borders.
author: Diaspora Desk
